stem: Which of the following is generally true regarding how different business entities are taxed for federal income tax purposes?

options.label: A
options.text: A C corporation is a pass-through entity that does not pay its own federal income tax.

options.label: B
options.text: An S corporation generally passes its income, losses, deductions, and credits through to its shareholders, subject to certain limitations.

options.label: C
options.text: A sole proprietorship must always file a separate federal income tax return from the owner.

options.label: D
options.text: A partnership’s income is taxed twice: once at the entity level and again when distributed to partners.

explanation: An S corporation is generally treated as a pass-through entity in which items of income, deduction, and credit flow through to shareholders, subject to eligibility and limitation rules. C corporations are subject to entity-level tax, and sole proprietorship income is reported directly on the owner's individual return.

stem: A calendar-year business purchases and places in service new 5-year MACRS property on July 1 of the current year. The business does not claim bonus depreciation or section 179. Under the general depreciation system and half-year convention, which of the following best describes the first-year depreciation?

options.label: A
options.text: A full 12 months of depreciation is allowed in the first year regardless of the convention.

options.label: B
options.text: One-half year of depreciation is allowed in the first year based on the appropriate 5-year MACRS percentage.

options.label: C
options.text: No depreciation is allowed in the first year; it begins in the second year.

options.label: D
options.text: The allowed depreciation is always prorated based on the exact number of days the asset was in service.

explanation: Under the half-year convention for 5-year MACRS property, the first year is treated as if the property were placed in service in the middle of the year, resulting in a half year of depreciation using the applicable MACRS percentage.

stem: Partner A contributes $20,000 cash to a partnership in exchange for a 50% interest. Partner B contributes depreciable property with an adjusted basis of $10,000 and a fair market value of $20,000, also for a 50% interest. The partnership has no liabilities immediately after formation. What is Partner B’s initial outside basis in the partnership interest?

options.label: D
options.text: $0, because no gain is recognized on contribution.

explanation: A partner’s initial outside basis in a partnership interest is generally the adjusted basis of property contributed plus any cash contributed. Here, Partner B’s basis is the adjusted basis of the contributed property, $10,000.

stem: An S corporation shareholder has a stock basis of $30,000 at the beginning of the year. During the year, the shareholder’s share of S corporation items includes $15,000 of ordinary income, $2,000 of tax-exempt income, and a $40,000 distribution. There are no other adjustments. What is the shareholder’s stock basis at the end of the year?

options.label: B
options.text: $0, and the entire distribution is taxable.

options.label: C
options.text: $5,000, and none of the distribution is taxable.

explanation: Stock basis in an S corporation is increased by income items (including tax-exempt income) and decreased by distributions (to the extent of basis) before considering losses. Beginning basis $30,000 + $15,000 ordinary income + $2,000 tax-exempt income = $47,000 adjusted basis, then minus the $40,000 distribution leaves $7,000 basis.

stem: A small consulting business incurs the following expenses: ordinary advertising costs, penalties paid to a government agency for late filing of a required report, and reasonable wages paid to the owner’s adult child for actual work performed. Which of the following statements is generally correct?

options.label: A
options.text: All three expenses are fully deductible as ordinary and necessary business expenses.

options.label: B
options.text: Advertising and reasonable wages may be deductible, but penalties paid to a government agency are generally nondeductible.

options.label: C
options.text: Penalties are deductible only if they do not exceed $5,000 per year.

options.label: D
options.text: Wages paid to a family member are never deductible, regardless of services performed.

explanation: Ordinary and necessary advertising expenses and reasonable wages for actual services are generally deductible. Fines and penalties paid to a government for violating the law are generally nondeductible.
